tldr: We propose AdaRoboVLG, an adaptive Vision-Language-Grasp (VLG) framework that decouples task understanding (foundation models) from physical grasp synthesis (base policy) via a structured interface, flexibly adapting to diverse robot hands and dynamic, cluttered environments without retraining the policy.
hero_caption: Comparison between conventional end-to-end VLG methods and our proposed AdaRoboVLG. (a) Real-world grasping involves compounded challenges such as cluttered scenes, functional requirements, and dynamic tracking. (b) Prior methods tightly couple these within a single network, limiting generalization. (c) AdaRoboVLG decouples contextual understanding via foundation models from physical grasp synthesis and connects them through a structured interface, achieving high adaptability.
overview:
Vision-Language-Grasp (VLG), enabling robots to pick objects based on verbal instructions, is a vital technology for deployment in homes and factories. In the real world, however, robots face simultaneous spatial, cognitive, and temporal challenges: grasping within cluttered environments full of obstacles, selecting functional parts tailored to subsequent use, and tracking moving objects. Conventional end-to-end models attempt to directly map images and instructions to grasp poses. This requires massive training datasets and makes adapting to new robot hands or unseen environments extremely difficult.

To address this, the authors turned their attention to human cognitive processes. Humans combine rich prior knowledge from past experiences to understand their surroundings, while maintaining generic physical motor skills for how to move their hands. Inspired by this, this paper introduces AdaRoboVLG, a framework that completely decouples task understanding from physical grasp synthesis. Bridging the two is a "structured grasp interface" comprising target object geometry, contact grasp representations (CGR), and grasp types.

On the grasp synthesis side, the framework builds a lightweight base policy that maps kinematics and evaluates force-closure stability. On the task understanding side, it combines DINOv3 (spatial prior), an LLM + SAM3 (cognitive prior), and SAM3 tracking + feature alignment (temporal prior) like plug-ins to dynamically update the interface.

Through simulations and real-world experiments, the authors confirm that the system deploys across 2-finger parallel grippers to 5-finger dexterous hands with high accuracy and zero retraining. In real-world tests, it achieved an 83.3% success rate across 102 objects in clutter, and demonstrated dynamic tracking and grasping of objects moving on a conveyor belt at 5 Hz.
contributions: Proposed AdaRoboVLG, an adaptive VLG framework that decouples contextual task understanding from physical grasp synthesis, mediated by a structured grasp interface.
Developed a highly generalizable base grasp policy using explicit kinematic mapping and a hand-agnostic hand-object interaction (HOI) representation to evaluate force-closure conditions.
Designed and integrated composable foundation-model prior modules that independently tackle cluttered scenes (spatial), functional instructions (cognitive), and dynamic tracking (temporal).

sections.heading: Why Grasping Is Hard: Moving Beyond the Limits of All-in-One Models
sections.summary: Real-world grasping involves an intricate mix of obstacle avoidance (spatial), intent-aligned part selection (cognitive), and dynamic object tracking (temporal). Existing end-to-end VLG models struggle to generalize by trying to solve all of this in a single network; this work proposes a new paradigm that separates task understanding from grasp synthesis.
sections.details:
Robotic grasping carries an inherent difficulty: selecting an appropriate pose from an infinite set of candidate contacts between the end-effector and the object. Moreover, real-world grasping is heavily context-dependent. For instance, executing "pick up the mug to pour" requires avoiding surrounding clutter, choosing the handle to support the downstream action (pouring versus handing over), and continuously adjusting the pose if the target moves.

Humans adapt smoothly without learning every situation from scratch by leveraging rich priors from common sense and past experience to guide perception and reasoning. Recently, foundation models have demonstrated powerful priors for visual recognition, spatial understanding, and reasoning, sparking widespread VLG research. However, most existing approaches rely on end-to-end models that output grasp poses directly from images and instructions. This paradigm is constrained by dataset coverage and computational demands, making it hard to scale across diverse robot hands and environmental shifts.

To tackle this challenge, AdaRoboVLG explicitly decouples task-dependent contextual understanding from physical grasp synthesis. Serving as the bridge is a "structured grasp interface" consisting of object geometry, Contact Grasp Representations (CGR), and grasp types drawn from human grasp taxonomy. Foundation models (spatial, cognitive, temporal) generate and update this interface according to the context, while a lightweight base policy transforms it into mechanically stable grasp poses. As a result, future advances in foundation models can directly enhance grasping capabilities without retraining the underlying policy.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of AdaRoboVLG. From multi-view RGB-D images and language instructions, the spatial, cognitive, and temporal prior modules construct and update the structured grasp interface. The base policy takes this interface, performs hand-specific candidate generation and hand-agnostic stability evaluation, and determines the final grasp pose.

sections.heading: Prior Footsteps: VLG, Multi-Fingered Grasping, and Foundation Models
sections.summary: We review related work across three areas: vision-language-conditioned grasping, learning-based multi-fingered grasp synthesis, and foundation models in robotics. AdaRoboVLG overcomes previous bottlenecks in generalization and deployability by decoupling task understanding from physical grasping and adopting hand-agnostic contact representations.
sections.details:
### Trends in Vision-Language Grasping (VLG)
Recent studies leverage LLMs or VLMs to extract affordances and spatial priors, or train Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models on large datasets to generate grasps directly from images and text. However, these models tend to be tightly coupled to specific hands and tasks, demanding additional data collection and retraining whenever transferring to a new hand or environment.

### Paradigms in Learning-Based Multi-Fingered Grasp Synthesis
Multi-fingered grasp synthesis broadly divides into hand-centric (regressing joint angles directly from observations), object-centric (predicting contact maps), interaction-centric (modeling hand-object relations), and scene-centric (handling cluttered environments). Yet, many suffer from heavy contact optimization costs or lock into a single hand geometry. AdaRoboVLG achieves both fast inference and cross-hand generalization by using explicit geometric mappings for candidate generation and hand-agnostic representations for evaluation.

### Foundation Models in Embodied AI
Foundation models are increasingly adopted in robotics via zero-shot transfer, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, or direct policy integration. In this work, DINOv3 and SAM3 are used zero-shot for geometry, semantics, and tracking, while an LLM is augmented with a taxonomy database for reliable reasoning, structured as plug-and-play modules feeding into the grasp interface.

sections.heading: Formulation and Core: The Structured Grasp Interface as a Shared Language
sections.summary: The grasp synthesis problem is decomposed into two stages: generating the interface from task context, and synthesizing executable poses from the interface. The interface consists of object geometry, local contact representations (CGR), and grasp types.
sections.details:
### Mathematical Formulation and Notation
A multi-fingered grasp pose $\bm{g}$ is defined by the robot wrist 6-DoF pose $\bm{T} \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ (rotation $\bm{R}$ and translation $\bm{t}$) and hand joint angles $\bm{q} \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The goal is to find a set of executable grasp poses $\mathcal{G}^{*}$ that satisfy the task context $\mathcal{C}$ and match the kinematic morphology of robot hand $\mathcal{H}$.

### Design of the Structured Grasp Interface
Rather than mapping context directly to grasp poses, this work formulates a two-stage synthesis through interface $\mathcal{I}$:
$$\mathcal{I} = f_{\tau}(\mathcal{C}), \quad \mathcal{G}^{*} = f_{\pi}(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{H})$$
Here, the interface is defined as $\mathcal{I} = (\mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{H}})$:
- $\mathcal{O}$: 3D object geometry (point cloud).
- $\mathcal{A} = \{\bm{a}_j\}$: A set of Contact Grasp Representations (CGR), serving as local contact primitives to establish stable grasps.
- $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{H}}$: A set of executable grasp types compatible with hand $\mathcal{H}$, based on human grasp taxonomy.

Because this interface acts as a neutral intermediary, the contextual module $f_{\tau}$ and the base grasp policy $f_{\pi}$ can be developed and refined completely independently.

captions.F3: Versatility of the Contact Grasp Representation (CGR). (a) From 2-finger parallel grippers to 5-finger hands, grasp poses can be synthesized sharing the same contact primitives. (b) It accommodates diverse grasp types from human grasp taxonomy, such as pinch, tripod, and wrap.

sections.heading: The Base Grasp Policy: Fast Kinematic Mapping and Hand-Agnostic Stability Scoring
sections.summary: The base policy consists of two stages: explicit kinematic mapping to rapidly generate hand-specific grasp candidates from CGRs and grasp types, and a hand-agnostic evaluation model to assess physical stability. Contact geometry is extracted as an HOI representation and scored via a PointTransformer-based network.
sections.details:
### Design Principles and CGR Definition
The base policy first generates hand-specific grasp candidates from the interface, then picks the most physically stable candidate. A CGR is defined as a tuple $\bm{a} = (\bm{p}_c, p, \bm{v}_a, \bm{v}_b, w)$, containing contact point $\bm{p}_c$, contact score $p$, approach vector $\bm{v}_a$, baseline closing vector $\bm{v}_b$, and grasp width $w$. This describes kinematic-agnostic geometric contact conditions.

### Hand-Specific Explicit Grasp Mapping
Using complex neural networks or heavy optimization for candidate generation slows down inference. Instead, leveraging hand closing synergies (where the first principal component accounts for 50-70% of variance), joint configurations are precomputed along a 1D manifold parameterized by grasp width $w$. By pre-calculating optimal joint angles $\bm{q}^*$ and transformation matrices to the Primary Closing Frame (PCF) as lookup tables offline, the policy generates candidate poses at runtime via simple table lookups and geometric transforms.

### HOI Representation and Hand-Agnostic Stability Evaluation
To judge whether candidates are physically stable, an interaction representation $\mathcal{R}^{\mathcal{HOI}}$ grounded in force-closure conditions (equilibrium within friction cones) is introduced. For contact points on the hand and object, point coordinates are centered on the object points and combined with surface normals and hand-side points/normals. Fed into a PointTransformer, a Contact-Aware Multi-Pooling (CAMP) module accommodates varying contact point counts and outputs a stability score $\beta \in [0, 1]$. Because inputs are normalized to local contact geometry, a single evaluation model reliably predicts stability across distinct hand morphologies.

captions.F4: Mechanism of hand-specific explicit grasp mapping. Joint configurations and reference frames (PCF) corresponding to grasp types and widths are precomputed offline as lookup tables, enabling fast and smooth candidate pose generation at runtime.
captions.F5: Hand-agnostic grasp evaluation module. HOI representations are extracted from contact interface geometry (points and normals). PointTransformer and CAMP pooling compute physical stability scores irrespective of hand shape or finger count.

sections.heading: Foundation Priors: Spatial, Cognitive, and Temporal Synergy
sections.summary: Three specialized modules address cluttered scenes (spatial), functional instructions (cognitive), and dynamic objects (temporal). Using DINOv3, LLM + SAM3, and feature-based tracking optimization, they dynamically update the shared structured grasp interface.
sections.details:
### Spatial Prior (Grasping in Clutter)
In dense scenes, the robot must identify collision-free approach paths. Dense semantic features are extracted from multi-view RGB images using DINOv3 and lifted to a 3D implicit field using depth. Contact-GraspNet is then applied to the scene point cloud to predict candidate CGRs $\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}$, establishing a collision-free grasp foundation.

### Cognitive Prior (Functional Grasping)
For instructions like "pick up the mug to pour," an LLM (Seed-1.8) is deployed. Because standard LLMs lack physical grasp grounding, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using a grasp taxonomy database is combined with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. This allows accurate deduction of target object (mug), functional part (handle), and grasp type (e.g., 3-finger pinch). The target part is grounded via SAM3 2D segmentation and lifted to 3D, filtering the spatial CGRs down to task-aligned functional candidates.

### Temporal Prior (Dynamic Grasp Tracking)
When objects move on a conveyor belt, grasp poses must update in real time. Under rigid-body assumptions, stable grasp poses remain invariant in the object's local frame. Using SAM3 video tracking to prevent ID switches, real-time 6-DoF motion $\bm{T}^{\mathcal{O}}_{0\to t}$ is estimated via gradient-based optimization matching initial 3D semantic features with the current feature field. Grasp poses update geometrically on the fly without re-running the base policy every frame, enabling agile tracking.

captions.F6: Spatial prior module pipeline. Multi-view RGB-D images are lifted to a 3D implicit feature field via DINOv3, working alongside Contact-GraspNet to extract scene geometry and executable candidate CGRs.
captions.F7: Cognitive prior module architecture. The LLM combines RAG and CoT to reason about grasp types and functional parts, followed by SAM3 visual grounding and 3D lifting to determine functional CGRs.

sections.heading: Simulation Results: Learning Efficiency, Generalization, and Strong Module Performance
sections.summary: Evaluation across 4.4 million trials in Isaac Sim showed that the base policy's HOI representation achieved strong cross-hand generalization. Meanwhile, the spatial, cognitive, and temporal modules outperformed state-of-the-art baselines in success rate and tracking accuracy.
sections.details:
### Data Collection and Base Policy Training
Using objects from GraspNet-1Billion, trial-and-error grasping simulations applying 0.5 N disturbance forces were conducted in Isaac Sim. Across three hands (DH3: 3-finger, Allegro: 4-finger, Inspire: 5-finger), 4.4 million stability samples were collected. The proposed HOI representation converged significantly faster than hand-object decoupled representations. When trained on mixed multi-hand data, the model achieved higher accuracy (DH3: 82.95%, Allegro: 88.02%, Inspire: 91.07%) than when trained on individual hands alone. t-SNE visualizations showed overlapping feature distributions across hands, confirming true morphology-independent stability evaluation.

### Individual Evaluation of Spatial, Cognitive, and Temporal Modules
- **Spatial Prior (DexGraspNet 2.0 Benchmark)**: In cluttered scenes, AdaRoboVLG achieved an 88.4% average success rate across all hands and difficulty splits, outperforming AnyDexGrasp by 3.0% on the Random split and 9.2% on the Loose split.
- **Cognitive Prior (Functional Grasp Reasoning & Language Grasping)**: On an open-set instruction dataset, RAG combined with CoT yielded 94.0% functional part accuracy and 87.0% grasp type accuracy. In simulated language-guided grasping, it surpassed AnyDexGrasp by 2.5-2.7% and beat $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O})$-Grasp by over 23%, achieving 81.3% on GraspClutter6D and 86.0% on GraspNet-1Billion.
- **Temporal Prior (Dynamic Grasp Tracking)**: On GraspNet-1Billion dynamic video sequences, it achieved a perfect Multi-Granularity Tracking Accuracy (MGTA) of 1.0 (no tracking loss or ID switches) and the lowest translation error among baselines. While asymmetric items like scissors tracked with millimeter-level precision, fully symmetric objects like strawberries or objects under severe initial occlusion showed slight pose drift.

sections.heading: Real-World Experiments: Functional, Dynamic Grasping in Challenging Setups
sections.summary: Validation was performed across three physical robot setups with two distinct end-effectors (a multi-fingered hand and a 2-finger gripper). AdaRoboVLG recorded an 83.3% success rate in static clutter and roughly 90% on moving conveyors and under aggressive human disturbances.
sections.details:
### Language-Guided Functional Grasping in Static Clutter
Experiments tested 102 daily objects across 6 categories (food, tools, groceries, etc.) with visually similar distractors placed around the target (510 trials total). AdaRoboVLG achieved an 83.3% overall success rate. It cleanly cleared dense obstacles around items like watermelons or toothpick containers, and selected intent-aligned parts and grasp types for tools like power drills and megaphones. Failure analysis showed errors were mostly due to misidentified functional parts (29.4%) or geometric depth noise (22.3%), rather than physical stability failures. Furthermore, swapping the multi-fingered hand for a 2-finger parallel gripper on a TianJi Marvin platform required zero retraining to execute functional grasps successfully.

### Dynamic Clutter and Human Disturbance Resistance
Using an AgileX Piper arm, objects moving on a conveyor at 2-5 cm/s were tracked and grasped. The system updated grasp poses in real time at 5 Hz, avoiding obstacles to secure cup handles via 3-finger pinches. When subjected to four types of severe human disturbances—rapid object translation, hand occlusion, and pulling objects completely out of frame (out-of-view recovery)—the system maintained an 89.7% average grasp success rate, showing strong robustness for deployment.

### Framework Extensibility
Because task understanding and grasp synthesis are separated, expanding functionality is straightforward. The authors demonstrated effortless scaling to bimanual sorting by appending a task allocator, and to transparent object grasping by integrating a depth restoration module (SwinDRNet)—all without retraining the policy.

sections.heading: Discussion and Conclusion: Decoupling Physics from Semantics
sections.summary: AdaRoboVLG attains high versatility and extensibility by loosely coupling foundation-model reasoning with a physical grasp policy. While limitations remain around perceptual noise, tactile feedback, and multi-stage manipulation, it provides a sustainable framework that directly benefits from future foundation model advancements.
sections.details:
### Current Limitations and Future Horizons
The authors outline three key areas for improvement:
- **Perceptual Uncertainty**: Depth sensor noise distorting contact geometry or multi-view segmentation mismatches can lead directly to grasp failures. Incorporating metric 3D reconstruction and dense point tracking will be essential.
- **Lack of Closed-Loop Tactile Control**: The base policy currently evaluates stability purely from visual geometry without tactile feedback upon contact. Slippage detection and reactive finger adjustments via tactile sensors are needed for delicate or slippery items.
- **Long-Horizon Tasks Beyond Single Grasps**: Handling heavily buried targets by pushing obstacles aside (non-prehensile actions) and chaining into downstream manipulation sequences remain crucial future steps.

### Conclusion
AdaRoboVLG establishes a clear division of labor: foundation models handle task understanding, while a lightweight, hand-agnostic base policy synthesizes physical grasps. This architecture avoids retraining massive policies from scratch, opening a scalable path where future foundation model breakthroughs instantly translate into sharper robotic grasping skills.

takeaways: Decoupling task understanding (LLMs/VLMs) from physical control (grasp synthesis) via a clean geometric and taxonomic interface proves far more scalable than end-to-end models.
Combining synergy-based kinematic lookup tables with an HOI representation normalized to contact points and normals enables a single base policy to evaluate stability across 2- to 5-finger hands.

Composing specialized foundation priors for static scenes (DINOv3), logical reasoning (LLMs with RAG and CoT), and dynamic tracking (SAM3 + feature alignment) provides modular adaptability to diverse real-world challenges.
limitations: Operates as an open-loop visual grasp policy, lacking tactile feedback for slip detection and dynamic force adjustment upon contact.
Upstream perceptual errors, such as depth sensor noise, pose drift on rotationally symmetric objects, or extreme occlusions, can directly trigger grasp failures.
Lacks integration with non-prehensile skills (e.g., pushing clutter aside) or multi-step manipulation planning for long-horizon tasks.
